Went to see The Odyssey.
A thoroughly entertaining 3 hours. 
Narratively Nolan plays it pretty straight - and in parts answers the question "what would a Tarantino movie directed by Nolan" look like.

The second viewing of The Odyssey just made me appreciate Nolan films even more due to his insistence of capturing everything IN camera. This is such a massive undertaking of filmmaking and a lot of directors would have taken the easy way to tell the story, but you can't fake people doing real shit.
I didn't see The Odyssey in IMAX, but it was in a 4:3 Aspect Ratio so I did see the entirety of Agamemnon's helmet mohawk as Nolan intended. Lol.

A post titled 'Movie of the week: The Odyssey (2026) - dir. Christopher Nolan'.

Text reads:

"I went to see this in a non-IMAX special screen that had rumbling, grumbling seats, and I do think that made me more excited. I liked being rumbled during tense moments. I also fell deeply in love with poor, gorgeous cyclops Polyphemus. He’s simply adorable. I really like him.

It was sort of funny that the emotional throughline of the movie was, essentially, another Oppenheimer moment (note to self: Odysseus x Oppenheimer slash fiction possible untapped market?), but what I loved was the general structure of the film, weaving through various jaw-dropping sequences and beautifully resonant scenes with incredible effects. Circe I am clapping and screaming at your antics. Do it again Circe.

Also, Tom Holland is my sweet son."

A post titled 'Album of the week: Night Talks - Running On A Cloud (2025)'.

The album cover sits at the top of the post - a purple background with a centred sword.

Text reads: 

"This is one of those albums that feels perfect for fast train journeys - watching hills and clouds roll by, progressing through the world in a blissful guitar haze, spotting a trio of horses in the blur of field. Real daydreaming music.

The rythmic, melancholic opening of ‘Nights’ transitions gorgeously into a beautiful BLAST of released anger and hard, crunchy guitar riff, then sinks back down into introspective self-soothing. A perfect anguished rock song.

More of an EP than an album, with seven smooth tracks, but they are lithe and danceable and raging and perfect."

I posted some more sculptures like this on my blog @

Wilson, a professor of classical studies at the University of Pennsylvania, said she didn't want to come across as a "snobby," nitpicking expert at odds with any deviation from the original text. But she questioned a range of omissions and other choices, from the absence on screen of the Gods Zeus and
Poseidon (Athena is played by Zendaya) to the "incoherent" messaging that condemns both war and physical cowardice. She found Penelope's role so thinned out that it endangered "any possibility of believing in this marriage." Wilson also that thought parts of the movie, notably the scenes with Odysseus' dog, Argos, "catered towards modern sentimentality." "Everybody's a sucker for a dog," she said.

"I spent a lot of time before I would write just familiarizing myself with the Odyssey... trying to remind myself what I remembered it to be."
"You get to the bit with Argus... his loyal hunting dog."
"As a new dog owner... I did not grow up with dogs."
"Finally got a dog... and yeah, changes your life."
"I got to the bit with Argus... and it just killed me."
"I think it was honestly a major reason that I knew I had to make the film."

While it's hard to say atm if I'd call this a modern masterpiece like so many others, I can confidently say that not only was this story a true match made in heaven (in a manner of speaking of course) for Christopher Nolan, but it is one of the best films I've ever seen in IMAX! I'm not kidding when I say that, for any and all issues I might've had (which I'll get to here in a sec) with the film which thankfully are very few and small relative to its strengths, it has to be seen in IMAX to get the absolute best experience! 

Although the film's pacing can drag a little bit in a few instances in the second half and Matt Damon's acting can come across as a bit too stoic at times, everything else from the all around strong acting, incredible score and sound design, gorgeous cinematography along with the sets and costume work, intense action that somehow manages to still feel brutal even without showing a lot of blood, to how surprisingly well they manage to adapt the more fantastical elements of the classic story in a more grounded setting without losing the heart and soul of Odysseus's journey, even if a few of them can straight up feel like right out of a twisted horror film in this adaptation.

All in all, while I can't pretend this adaptation will win everyone over (though it certainly has for a lot of people this far) it is worth checking if for no other reason than to see all the hard work that went into making something that truly feels like a modern epic in a lot of ways, especially for IMAX! Much like Odysseus's tale, it's sure to be a story that'll be talked about for years to come!

Saw The Odyssey. A good, not great movie. I’d give it 6.5 out of 10. Probably better in the theater.

Some more thoughts:

This is The Odyssey of Nolan, not The Odyssey of Homer. They say artists steal, b/c that’s how you make something your own. If you go in wanting Homer, you’ll be disappointed.

Chris Nolan, I took my beautiful son to see The Odyssey and he dressed up as his favorite character, a big bag of wind. He left crying because you wrote him out. You have no respect for Homer or Western Civilization.
Nolan understands that you can hang a lot more off the story of the Odyssey but that the Iliad is infinitely more interesting thematically, lol.

My favorite part about the Odyssey resurgence is how Emily Wilson and Christopher Nolan settled a 28 year dispute between my Pre-Ap World Studies teacher and I on the proper pronunciation of Telemachus. I’m finally vindicated on the correct pronunciation.
Went in skeptical cause Nolan can be hit or miss for me but… The Odyssey is a masterpiece
